content: Erythromycin is an antibiotic that is used to treat a wide range of bacterial infections. It may also be prescribed to prevent certain bacterial infections. This medication belongs to a class of drugs known as macrolide antibiotics. It is important to note that erythromycin is effective only against bacterial infections and will not work for viral infections, such as the common cold or flu. This medication is typically administered by injection into a vein as directed by your doctor, usually every six hours. The injection should be given slowly over a period of 20 to 60 minutes. It is recommended to use this injectable form only until you are able to take an oral antibiotic or until your treatment is completed. If you are administering this medication at home, ensure that you have been properly trained by a healthcare professional on how to prepare and use it. Before using, visually inspect the product for particles or discoloration; do not use the liquid if either is present. For optimal effectiveness, erythromycin should be used at evenly spaced intervals. If you are using this medication to treat an infection, it is crucial to complete the full prescribed course, even if symptoms improve after a few days. Stopping the medication too early may result in the infection returning. If you are using this medication to prevent certain bacterial infections, follow your doctor’s instructions precisely. Common side effects of erythromycin include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea or loose stools, stomach pain, and pain or redness at the injection site. Remember that this medication has been prescribed because your doctor has determined that the benefits outweigh the risks of side effects. Rarely, erythromycin may cause a severe intestinal condition known as Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea, which can occur during treatment or weeks to months after treatment has stopped. Prolonged or repeated use of this medication may lead to oral thrush or a new vaginal yeast infection. Serious allergic reactions to this drug are rare but possible. Before using erythromycin, inform your doctor or pharmacist if you are allergic to it, to other macrolide or ketolide antibiotics (such as clarithromycin or azithromycin), or if you have any other allergies. This product may contain inactive ingredients that could cause allergic reactions or other problems. Erythromycin may interfere with the effectiveness of live bacterial vaccines, such as the typhoid vaccine. Additionally, this medication may cause a condition that affects the heart rhythm, known as QT prolongation. The risk of QT prolongation may be higher if you have certain medical conditions or are taking other drugs that can cause QT prolongation. Low levels of potassium or magnesium in the blood may also increase this risk, especially if you are using certain medications like diuretics or experiencing conditions such as severe sweating, diarrhea, or vomiting. Infants may be at a higher risk for a serious stomach condition when using this medication. During pregnancy, erythromycin should only be used when clearly needed, as it passes into breast milk. Drug interactions may alter how erythromycin or other medications work or increase the risk of serious side effects. Keep a list of all the products you use, including prescription and non-prescription drugs and herbal products, and share it with your doctor and pharmacist. Erythromycin can affect the removal of other medications from your body, potentially altering their effectiveness. It may also interfere with certain laboratory tests, such as urine tests, leading to false results. In the event of an overdose, if someone has serious symptoms such as passing out or difficulty breathing, call emergency services immediately (911 in the U.S.). Otherwise, contact a poison control center right away. U.S. residents can call 1-800-222-1222. While using this medication, your doctor may order laboratory or medical tests to monitor your progress and check for side effects. Be sure to attend all medical and lab appointments. If you miss a dose, contact your doctor or pharmacist promptly to establish a new dosing schedule. For storage, consult the product instructions and your pharmacist for specific details. Do not flush medications down the toilet or pour them into a drain unless instructed to do so. Properly discard this product when it is expired or no longer needed. This information is a summary and does not include all possible details about erythromycin. It does not guarantee that this product is safe, effective, or appropriate for you. Always consult your healthcare professional for complete information about this medication and your specific health needs.
